More than 17 million people in Germany work in offices, and half of them are unhappy with the acoustics. Since May 2019, Benjamin Müller has pursued a doctorate on the problem in the Psychoacoustics and Cognitive Ergonomics group of the Fraunhofer Institute for Building Physics (IBP) in Stuttgart, a project he expects to take six years. In lab and field studies with participants, he evaluates actively designed soundscapes for open-plan offices and develops new methods, from software and sound masking to measurement procedures.

Fraunhofer’s strongly applied research hooked him during a 2015 internship at the Soundlab of Fraunhofer IIS in Erlangen, while he studied multimedia and communication at Ansbach University. During a master’s at Stuttgart Media University he joined IBP next door, as a student assistant from 2017 and a research associate since 2018. He is now also a business developer for his department.

The challenges are real: with no ready-made projects, he must win funding himself, juggle many topics, take three civil engineering modules (4 ECTS each) for the University of Stuttgart, and write the thesis largely in his own time. The rewards include a feel for real market needs and two patents now heading toward licensing. He has supervised theses since 2019 and taught at Ansbach since 2021. His advisor is Professor Leistner, head of Fraunhofer IBP and the University of Stuttgart’s IABP; the degree requires at least three peer-reviewed papers besides the monograph. He recommends Fraunhofer to those with time, realistic expectations and a taste for applied research.

Adapted into Chinese by Fanyu Meng from Benjamin Müller’s first-person profile in Akustik Journal, published by the German Acoustical Society (DEGA).
